column1: Why must smart contract execution be universally deterministic across all validators?
column2: Because validators with different hardware, OS kernels, and runtime versions must arrive at byte-identical state after processing the same transaction; any divergence (e.g., a timestamp read or float rounding difference) would fork the chain into irreconcilable branches.

column1: List five sources of non-determinism that smart contract VMs must eliminate.
column2: System clock access, hardware random number generation, floating-point arithmetic, concurrent thread scheduling, and network I/O with variable latency.

column1: How do smart contract platforms guarantee halting despite the undecidability of the halting problem?
column2: Through an economic mechanism (gas metering) rather than static analysis: every transaction carries a finite resource budget, and execution is forcibly terminated when that budget is exhausted.

column1: What does the FLP impossibility theorem prove, and why does it matter for blockchain consensus?
column2: It proves no deterministic protocol can guarantee both safety and liveness in an asynchronous system where even one process may fail; as a result, every production consensus mechanism (e.g., Ethereum's Gasper) is a compromise that trades unconditional guarantees for safety under honest supermajority and liveness under partial synchrony.

column1: Distinguish probabilistic finality from cryptoeconomic finality in Ethereum's post-Merge design.
column2: Probabilistic finality emerges from block confirmation depth, where reorg cost grows exponentially with each added block. Cryptoeconomic finality is provided by Casper FFG's two-phase justify/finalize checkpoint process requiring a supermajority (>2/3 staked ETH) of attestations each epoch.

column1: Why is a 'confirmed' transaction better understood as a probability distribution rather than a binary state?
column2: Because blockchain finality is probabilistic and strengthens over time as more validators attest and the fork-choice rule raises the economic cost of rewriting history — unlike a serializable database commit, which is instantaneously binary.

column1: Why can't blockchains use the naive approach of hashing a sorted serialized blob of all key-value state?
column2: Because a single storage write would invalidate the hash and require re-serializing and re-hashing potentially gigabytes of state; Merkle trees instead localize updates to O(log n) nodes along the path from leaf to root.

column1: What is the state_root and why must it be identical across all full nodes?
column2: A 32-byte hash committing to the entire world state, embedded in the block header; if even one storage slot differs between nodes, their state roots diverge and the chain forks.

column1: What is the mechanical root cause of reentrancy in the EVM?
column2: When a contract issues a CALL, execution suspends but storage is not frozen — slots updated before the call reflect new values while slots not yet updated retain stale values, creating an inconsistent state visible to a reentering callee.

column1: What two implicit programming assumptions does reentrancy violate?
column2: That an external call is atomic and side-effect-contained from the caller's perspective, and that your own function's execution is uninterruptible — neither holds in the EVM since external calls hand control to arbitrary code that can call back in.

column1: State the Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) pattern and explain why the ordering is non-negotiable.
column2: First verify preconditions (checks), then write all state changes (effects), then perform external calls (interactions). This ordering prevents an external callee from re-entering the function while effects are only partially applied.

column1: Why does smart contract security demand aerospace/medical-firmware-level formal rigor compared to typical software?
column2: Because blockchain execution is economically final and irreversible — a violated invariant doesn't just produce a bug report or rollback, it produces a permanent, unrecoverable transfer of funds to an attacker.
